::: {.why}
The slope you measured last night is a known result, and knowing it tells you exactly how much more often you would have to trade to halve your hedging risk, which is the input to the cost trade-off tomorrow.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- State the rate at which hedging error falls with rebalancing frequency and confirm it from your simulation.
- Describe the distribution of hedging error, and say why it is not symmetric for a short option.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>65 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Confirm the rate: the standard deviation of hedging error falls as the reciprocal of the square root of the number of rebalances. Fit the slope on log axes from your simulation and check it matches. Then say what that implies: halving the error costs four times the trading.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Look at the shape rather than only the spread: plot the histogram of hedging profit for a short option and note the skew. A short gamma position loses on large moves and wins slowly, which produces exactly the return distribution that looks excellent in a backtest and is not.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Connect it back: that shape is the same one you would get from any strategy that sells insurance, and your day 47 drawdown work applies to it directly.
:::
:::
